sections.title: Shorter ways to say "if"
sections.content: You know *si* + the imperfect subjunctive from B1 Unit 4 and *si* + the pluperfect subjunctive from B1 Unit 35. A condition does not always need *si*. Spanish can state it with *de* + infinitive, or with a gerund, which is shorter and sounds more written. With *de* + infinitive the main clause shows the time: *De tener tiempo, iría contigo* means *Si tuviera tiempo, iría contigo*, and *De haberlo sabido, habría venido* means *Si lo hubiera sabido, habría venido*. A real condition works too: *De ser necesario, te llamo* means *Si es necesario, te llamo*. A gerund can also carry the condition: *Estudiando más, aprobarías* means *Si estudiaras más, aprobarías*.

sections.title: Four patterns
rows: If I had time, I would go with you. (= Si tuviera tiempo…)
Had I known, I would have come. (= Si lo hubiera sabido…)
De no llegar a tiempo, te llamaré.
If I do not arrive in time, I will call you. (= Si no llego a tiempo…)
If you studied more, you would pass. (= Si estudiaras más…)

items.spanish: De ser necesario, te llamo mañana.
items.english: If necessary, I will call you tomorrow.

items.spanish: De haber previsto el problema, habríamos cambiado el plan.
items.english: Had we foreseen the problem, we would have changed the plan.

items.spanish: Hablando con calma, todos se entenderían mejor.
items.english: If everyone spoke calmly, they would understand each other better.

sections.content: The *de* or gerund phrase comes first, followed by a comma. After *de* the verb is always an infinitive: *De haberlo sabido*, never *De hubiera sabido*. The pronoun attaches to the infinitive: *haberlo*. A gerund condition normally shares its subject with the main clause: you study, and you pass.
